title: Controls at a glance
text:
Drag from the launch planet to aim: the direction sets the launch angle and the drag length sets the power. The arrow keys also aim (left and right turn, up and down change power; hold Shift for fine steps). Press Enter or Space to launch, R to reset and retry, S for slow motion, N to add a burn node, Tab to select a node, Delete to remove it, and the mouse wheel to zoom. Press H to open Navigator.

Try: aim with a drag, then fine-tune with Shift and the arrow keys while watching the preview line.

title: Units and mu
text:
This game uses simplified physics in game units, not real ones. The gravitational constant is 1, so a body's mu equals its mass, and the pull it exerts at distance r is mu divided by r squared. Distances are in game units and speeds are in units per second. Everything in these guides describes the game's own physics. Heavier bodies have a larger mu: in the early levels Home has mu 20, Kepi has mu 14 or 30, and the star Sol has mu 1000.

Try: open a calculator question, such as asking for the circular speed here, to see mu used in real numbers.

title: Reading the preview line
text:
The preview shows where the probe will go over the next 15 seconds. It is not an estimate: it uses the same physics step as the real flight, so a launch follows its preview exactly, including burn nodes. A teal line means the path is safe. An orange line with a ring means the path ends in a crash, and the ring marks where. The preview updates every time you change the aim or a node, and during flight it restarts from the probe's current position.

Try: change one thing at a time and watch how the line moves before you commit to a launch.

title: Fuel and delta-v
text:
Launching is free. Only burn nodes cost fuel, and a burn costs exactly its delta-v, which is the length of its change in velocity: the square root of prograde squared plus radial squared. The total of all burns cannot exceed the level's tank, and the game scales a drag down to what is left. Running out of fuel is not a failure, because the probe simply coasts. Par fuel is what the designer's solution used, and finishing at or below par earns three stars.

Try: look for a plan with fewer or smaller burns before adding more.

title: Asteroid fields
text:
An asteroid field is a ring of small rocks orbiting a body. The rocks follow fixed orbits, so they move the same way every attempt, and they do not pull on the probe, but touching one is a crash. The preview shows your path crossing the field, and a crash marker if it hits a rock. Passing outside the ring or inside its inner edge is safe, and crossing quickly at a steady course gives the rocks less time to line up with you. The timing of your arrival matters because the rocks keep moving.

Try: check the preview for an orange marker inside the ring and shift your launch time or angle until it clears.

title: Solar wind
text:
A solar wind zone pushes the probe with a steady force while it is inside, and the direction of the push turns slowly over time. The push fades smoothly near the edge of the zone, so there is no sudden jolt. The preview already includes the wind, so the line you see is the path you will fly. You can use the push on purpose: aim so that it carries you onto the target, or burn against it. The longer you stay inside the zone, the more it moves you.

Try: watch how the preview bends inside the zone and aim off to one side so the wind carries you back.

title: Dark mass
text:
A dark mass is a tiny body with an enormous pull. Flying past it can fling the probe a long way with no fuel, which makes it a strong gravity assist, but a path that comes too close is a crash because its surface is very small. Near it the probe moves very fast, tens of units per second, so keep your closest approach comfortably wide: the farther the pass, the gentler and more predictable the bend. Use the preview to check the closest-approach pin before you commit.

Try: increase the miss distance a little at a time and watch the bend and the closest-approach label.

title: Level 1: First Light
text:
Reach Kepi and stay close to it for 4 seconds, anywhere between 0.8 and 2.5 units from it. Kepi has mu 14, so it can catch a probe that arrives slowly enough. A launch at about 82 degrees with power near 5.5 works: aim a little ahead of Kepi, not straight at it, because it moves while you fly. You do not need any burns, so the par fuel is zero. If the probe flies past, lower the power slightly.

Try: start from 82 degrees at about 80 percent power, then adjust with Shift and the arrow keys.

title: Level 2: Falling Around
text:
Kepi is heavier here (mu 30) and starts on a different side, so it holds on to the probe more strongly. The goal is to stay between 0.8 and 3.5 units of Kepi for 6 seconds. A launch near 246 degrees at power about 5.4 works with no burns. Because the pull is stronger, a probe that arrives too fast can still bend into a loop, so the path often curves around Kepi on the preview. Par fuel is zero.

Try: aim near 246 degrees at about 77 percent power and check that the preview curls around Kepi.

title: Level 3: Burn Nodes
text:
The hold time here is 12 seconds, between 0.8 and 3.5 units of Kepi, which a launch alone cannot manage: the probe swings past and leaves. Launch near 156 degrees at power about 6.25, then add one node about 5.6 seconds into the flight, close to the moment of closest approach, with a small retrograde burn of about 0.3. Any time between about 4.8 and 6.4 seconds works. Par fuel is 0.3.

Try: add the node by clicking the path near the closest approach, then drag the brass handle backward.

title: What a burn node is
text:
A burn node is an instant change in velocity at a chosen time after launch. Click the preview line, or press N, to add one. Select it to show two handles: brass for prograde and teal for radial. Drag a handle to set the delta-v, or use plus and minus for prograde and comma and period for radial. Each node costs fuel equal to its delta-v and levels limit how many nodes you can place. The preview updates live, and you can edit future nodes during flight.

Try: add a node, drag one handle a little, and read the change in the preview.

title: A burn at apoapsis raises the periapsis
text:
Speeding up at one point of an orbit raises the opposite side of it. A prograde burn at the apoapsis lifts the periapsis, which is the standard way to turn a stretched ellipse into a rounder orbit, and a prograde burn at periapsis raises the apoapsis. Burning where the probe is slowest and farthest is the most efficient place to change the periapsis. A transfer between two circular orbits uses one burn to leave the first and a second to settle into the next.

Try: if your path dips into a planet, add a small prograde node on the far side of the loop.

title: Slowing down to be captured
text:
Arriving fast at a moon means moving above its escape speed relative to it, so gravity bends the path but does not hold you. A retrograde burn near the closest approach lowers your speed relative to the moon, which makes the orbit bound. Even a small burn can be enough, and timing is forgiving because anywhere near the closest approach works. In level 3 a retrograde burn of about 0.3 around 5.6 seconds after launch works, and any time from about 4.8 to 6.4 seconds does too.

Try: click the path near where it passes the moon and drag the brass handle backward.

title: Slow motion planning
text:
Press S during flight to slow time to one tenth speed. The budget is measured in real seconds and is shown in the HUD, so use it where precision matters, such as dragging a node's handle near a close pass. Slow motion does not change the physics, only how fast you watch it, so the flight and the preview stay identical. When the budget runs out, time returns to normal automatically.

Try: save slow motion for placing a burn just before a close approach.

title: Radial burns
text:
A radial burn is perpendicular to your motion, so it turns your velocity rather than speeding it up or slowing it down. That makes it useful for small course corrections, for example to shift a close pass a little to one side. It costs fuel in the same way as any burn, equal to its delta-v. To change the size of an orbit, prograde and retrograde burns are more direct, and combining both lets you aim and adjust speed together.

Try: if the path misses the target by a little, try a small radial burn early in the flight.

title: The orbit delivery mission
text:
To deliver the cargo you must keep the probe inside a radius band around the target body for the full hold time without a break. Leaving the band resets the timer to zero, and the HUD shows your progress as a percentage. The mission line gives the target, the inner and outer radius of the band, and the hold time. A near-circular orbit inside the band is the safest way to finish, because an elongated orbit leaves the band on every lap.

Try: compare the band's middle radius with the circular speed there to judge the orbit you need.

title: Stars and payouts
text:
Completing a level earns one star. Using fuel at or below 125 percent of par earns two, and at or below par earns three, where par is the fuel used by the designer's stored solution. Payout adds a base amount, a bonus for fuel left in the tank, and a small bonus for finishing quickly. A crash or leaving the map pays nothing, but you can retry instantly. Many early levels have a par of zero, so a launch without burns is already a perfect score.

Try: after a win, retry with fewer or smaller burns to reach three stars.

title: Rendezvous with a station
text:
A rendezvous succeeds when the probe is within the capture distance of the station and its speed relative to the station is below the limit. The station is moving, so what counts is the difference between your velocity and its velocity, not your speed against the sky. A fast pass through the capture area is not a capture: the probe keeps flying and you can try again. The HUD shows the gap and the relative speed while you fly. Arriving at the right time matters as much as the right path.

Try: aim to arrive alongside the station, then use a small burn to match its speed as the gap closes.

title: Soft landing
text:
To land you must touch the target's surface slower than the landing limit, measured relative to the surface, so a moving moon counts its own motion. Touching it any faster is a crash, and so is touching any other body at any speed. Gravity speeds you up as you fall, so slow down early: a retrograde burn well before touchdown works better than a hard burn at the last moment. The HUD shows your altitude and speed against the limit.

Try: add a retrograde node before the descent and check the preview's closing speed.

title: Gate run
text:
A gate run asks you to fly through a series of gates in order. A gate is a short bar between two posts, and the probe passes it when its path crosses the bar. Crossing a later gate out of order does not count, but it does not end the attempt either: you can come back and cross it again once it is next. The next gate is shown in gold, finished gates in teal, and the HUD tells you which gate is next. Passing around the end of a bar does not count.

Try: place nodes so the preview line crosses each bar in turn, in order.

title: Crashing into a body
text:
A crash happens when the probe comes closer to a body's center than its radius. The preview shows it before you launch: an orange line ending in a ring. Common causes are a launch power that is too low, so the probe falls back onto its own planet, or a close pass whose closest point is below the target's surface. To fix it, raise the closest point of the path with a prograde burn on the far side, or change the aim so the path passes farther from the body.

Try: look at the orange ring and move the aim until the line misses the body.

title: Leaving the map
text:
If the probe travels beyond the map bounds, the attempt ends with a message saying how long it took. This usually means the launch power was too high or an assist threw the probe outward. If your launch power is above the escape speed of the planet you left, the probe will not fall back. Lower the power a little, or add a retrograde burn to slow down. The preview turns orange and the message line says the launch leaves the map before you fly.

Try: reduce power by about ten percent and check the preview again.

title: Flying past the target
text:
If the probe passes the target and keeps going, it arrived faster than the target's escape speed. Gravity bent the path but could not hold it. Arrive more slowly by launching with a bit less power, or burn retrograde near the closest approach. Aiming a little ahead of a moving target helps too, because it will have moved by the time you arrive. A close pass that hugs the surface bends the path more than a distant one but risks a crash.

Try: lower the launch power slightly, or add a small retrograde node near the target.

title: Cannot hold the orbit band
text:
The hold timer restarts whenever the probe leaves the radius band, so an orbit that swings out of the band each lap never finishes. This happens when the orbit is too elongated, with a periapsis below the inner radius or an apoapsis beyond the outer one. Aim for a near-circular orbit at the middle of the band. Adjust it with a burn at the periapsis or apoapsis: a prograde burn raises the opposite side and a retrograde burn lowers it.

Try: compare the preview's periapsis and apoapsis with the band edges, then burn to bring them closer together.

title: Gravity and bodies on rails
text:
Planets, moons, and stations move on fixed Kepler orbits around their parents. They are not pulled by the probe, so their motion is the same every attempt. The probe, however, feels every body at once: the star, the planet you launched from, and the target moon. The nearest and heaviest body usually dominates, but far bodies still add small pulls, which is why a path can drift. Because bodies keep moving, the same launch can work at one moment and miss at another.

Try: watch where the target will be when you arrive, not where it is now.

title: Circular orbit speed
text:
At distance r from a body with parameter mu, the speed that gives a circular orbit is the square root of mu divided by r. For example, around Kepi in level 2 (mu 30) at r = 1.5 the circular speed is about 4.47. Faster than that and the orbit stretches into an ellipse that reaches farther out. Slower and it dips closer to the body. A circular orbit keeps the same distance, so it is the easiest way to stay inside a radius band.

Try: ask Navigator for the circular speed here to get the number for the current level.

title: Escape speed
text:
Escape speed at distance r is the square root of 2 times mu divided by r, which is about 1.41 times the circular speed there. Above it the probe never falls back: it flies on in an open path. From Home's pad (r about 0.84, mu 20) escape speed is about 6.9, and the launch power limit is 7. Relative to a moon, escape speed is much lower, so a probe arriving fast will fly past it rather than orbit.

Try: when a launch leaves the map or flies past the target, lower the power a little.

title: Orbit shapes, periapsis and apoapsis
text:
A bound orbit is an ellipse. The closest point to the body is the periapsis and the farthest is the apoapsis. If they are equal the orbit is circular. The probe moves fastest at periapsis and slowest at apoapsis. If the probe's energy is above zero, the path is open and has no apoapsis: it escapes. The preview reports the orbit it would settle into, so you can check the periapsis stays above the body's surface.

Try: if the periapsis is below the surface the path will crash; raise it with a burn on the far side of the orbit.

title: Orbital period
text:
The time for one lap of a circular orbit of radius r is 2 pi times the square root of r cubed divided by mu. Around Kepi in level 2 (mu 30) at r = 1.5 one lap takes about 2.1 seconds, so holding the band for 6 seconds is about three laps. Closer orbits are faster and farther orbits slower. Knowing the period helps you judge whether a hold time is realistic and when the probe will next pass the same point.

Try: ask Navigator for the period at the radius you plan to orbit.

title: Prograde, retrograde and radial
text:
Burn directions are measured against the probe's velocity relative to the body that pulls on it most. Prograde is along that velocity, so a prograde burn speeds you up. Retrograde is the opposite, so it slows you down. Radial is perpendicular to the velocity and points away from the body. The two handles on a selected node are the brass prograde axis and the teal radial axis. Dragging a handle backward through the node gives a retrograde burn.

Try: use prograde or retrograde to change your orbit's size, and radial to nudge its direction.

title: What a gravity assist is
text:
A planet or moon moves along its orbit, and when the probe passes it the pull bends the probe's path. Measured against the moving body, the probe leaves with the same speed it arrived with, only in a new direction. But the body itself is moving, so measured against the star the probe's speed and direction change. Passing behind a body that moves in your direction can speed you up, and passing in front of it can slow you down, all without burning fuel.

Try: look at the preview as you move the aim, and see how a pass near a moving body bends the path.

title: Saving fuel with an assist
text:
A well-timed flyby can replace a burn. If the path needs a change of speed or direction, check whether passing a body would give it for free before spending fuel. Keep the closest point above the body's surface, because a pass that gets too low becomes a crash. Assists depend on timing, because the body must be in the right place when you arrive. Fuel above one and a half times par is a sign to look for one, and later levels are built around them.

Try: compare a plan with a node to one that bends around a planet, and keep the cheaper one.

title: Launch angle and power
text:
The launch angle chooses the direction and the power sets the speed relative to the planet. Power up to 7 is allowed, and escape speed from Home's pad is about 6.9. In the early levels, powers between roughly 5 and 6.3 reach the moon with a manageable speed. Small changes matter: a power change of 0.03 can shift where you arrive by a lot, so make small adjustments and check the preview. Angle decides where the path crosses the moon's orbit.

Try: set the angle first so the path crosses the target's orbit, then tune the power.

title: Making fine adjustments
text:
Dragging is good for rough aiming and the arrow keys are good for fine control. Holding Shift makes the steps much smaller: about 0.01 radians for the angle and about 0.02 speed units for the power. Change only one thing at a time, then read the preview. If a path almost works, try the smallest step in each direction and see which way it improves. Slow motion is available in flight for node handles.

Try: when the path is close, switch from dragging to Shift plus the arrow keys.
